extracted.intended_audience: engineers, manufacturers, ordnance/mining professionals and informed general readers interested in explosive manufacture and handling
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and safety-oriented guidance for producing, processing, transporting, storing, and firing various explosives (gunpowder, nitro-glycerine, dynamite, gun-cotton, explosive gelatine). Includes manufacturing recipes, process conditions, and desired performance/safety characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saltpeter quality and purification
rubrics_metrics.description: Select saltpeter with great care; procure from reliable sources or prepare artificially and purify by dissolving in hot water and recrystallization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saltpeter is obtained naturally (India) or prepared artificially by mixing earth with decomposing organic matter, allowing crystals to form, then extracting and evaporating. If crude, repeat purification to obtain a fine white powder of proper fineness for gunpowder manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charcoal quality for gunpowder
rubrics_metrics.description: Charcoal must be prepared carefully; high nearly-pure carbon content and low ash lead to more violent action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use very light woods (black alder, willow) stripped of bark; roast in a retort at uniform heat with free exit of vapors and withdraw before overburning. Proper charcoal is bluish-black, slightly elastic, slightly resonant, with clear wood fiber—different from ordinary charcoal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sulphur preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare sulphur from its ore by roasting and condensing vapors into liquid sulphur, then harden in molds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roast ore in retort, condense vapors, run into molds and allow to solidify to obtain material suitable for powder manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fineness, proportions, and moisture during incorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ingredients must be of proper fineness and in desired proportions; mixed while moist enough to be like dough but not too wet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pulverize charcoal and sulphur with bronze/zinc balls; then mix saltpeter and incorporate in an incorporating mill (iron wheels) while moist. Excess water interferes with proper mixture; aim for dough-like consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milling, pressing, and granulation techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate mills, presses, and granulators to mix, press, break, and size the powder; avoid dangerous equipment choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating mill with revolving iron wheels mixes and presses; dry the mill-cake, break between heavy wooden rollers, press in a hydraulic press (avoid screw-press to prevent friction ignition), granulate through rollers and sieves, remove dust on wire gauze, and glaze grains in a slow drum with plumbago if required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid iron tools and separate buildings for safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Handle finished powder and operations with non-sparking tools and conduct hazardous operations in separate buildings at safe distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finished powder packed in oak kegs with copper hoops; use no iron tool when opening. Conduct operations in buildings sufficiently distant from each other to prevent chain explosions; locate plants along streams for power but spaced apart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grain size, shape, and density control burning rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Burning rate of gunpowder is affected by grain size (larger grains burn slower), grain shape (affects surface area and packing), and density (lower density burns faster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust granule size and shape to obtain desired combustion characteristics; density depends on press-cake pressure—control pressing to tune rapidity of burning and strain on gun walls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alternative explosive mixtures constrained by sensitivity/corrosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Other explosive mixtures may be prevented from use by greater sensitivity to friction/percussion or by corrosive effects on gun metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider safety and compatibility with metal when evaluating alternative explosive compositions; enhanced power may be offset by dangerous sensitivity or corrosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nitration temperature control for nitro-glycerine manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain low temperature (not above ~48° F) during nitration of glycerine with nitric and sulphuric acids to avoid fire or explosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ice bath around acid pitchers, agitate constantly, monitor each pitcher frequently with a thermometer. Sulphuric acid must absorb water formed to keep nitric acid at normal strength. Excessive temperature risks ignition of newly formed nitro-glycerine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of reactants for nitro-glycerine (glycerine quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pure, redistilled glycerine; impure glycerine makes nitro-glycerine much more dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many accidents stem from inferior glycerine; insist on high-quality glycerine (a by-product of stearine candles) and remove impurities by redistillation before nitration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Washing and removal of acid for stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly wash nitro-glycerine and gun-cotton to remove residual acids; presence of acid causes decomposition and spontaneous explosions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pour nitrated product through strainer into agitated water vats, allow nitro-glycerine to settle, draw off acid water, and wash repeatedly until pure. For gun-cotton, use centrifugal strainers and prolonged washing until acid-water no longer remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling, storage and transportation of nitro-glycerine (use absorbents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because liquid nitro-glycerine is dangerously liable to leak and explode in transport, mix with absorbents (e.g., siliceous earth) to form dynamite for safer handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absorbent (siliceous earth) mixed about three parts earth to one part nitro-glycerine by weight; prevent exudation by controlling nitro-glycerine proportion. Be aware dynamite freezes at ~40° F and may need thawing before use; never heat carelessly (no red-hot poker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of dynamite and mixtures: absorbent choice and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Select an inert absorbent and proper proportions to avoid exudation and to permit safe handling without reducing explosive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dynamite typically uses diatomaceous siliceous earth. Do not put too much nitro-glycerine into the absorbent. Other mixtures (charcoal, sawdust, chlorate, gunpowder) generally add little and may increase danger. Cellulose dynamite (nitro-treated wood-pulp) is preferred for water resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freezing and thawing considerations for explosives
rubrics_metrics.description: Some explosives (nitro-glycerine, dynamite, gun-cotton) freeze or change state at ~40° F; frozen state affects ignition/detonation behavior and may require thawing by safe methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frozen nitro-glycerine is difficult and uncertain to fire; dynamite frozen in a compact mass is hard to explode while powdery frozen dynamite may still detonate. Thaw by safe warm water (not open flame or red-hot metal). Avoid procedures that increase risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wet vs dry state handling of gun-cotton
rubrics_metrics.description: Gun-cotton is safer for transport when wet (hard to detonate) but must be dried for use or detonated with a dry primer; wet gun-cotton rapidly absorbs moisture and primers are difficult to keep dry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacture includes nitration, centrifugal straining, prolonged washing, pulping, and pressing. Carry gun-cotton wet for safety; dry primers are used to detonate wet gun-cotton. Consider commercial disadvantages due to moisture sensitivity and cost of waterproof cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primer/firing requirements for high explosives
rubrics_metrics.description: High explosives generally require a fulminate primer or similar detonator; the characteristics of the primer (type, grain amount) determine reliable detonation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fulminate of mercury (wet for safety) is commonly used; typical fulminate quantities cited: 15–25 grains to detonate nitro-glycerine, about 25 grains to detonate gelatine with a dry gun-cotton fuse. Electrical primers use a bridge wire (platinum-silver) heated by current to ignite a gun-cotton wisp in contact with fulminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and construction of an electric detonator
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct detonators with a metal cylinder partially filled with wet fulminate, plug containing two insulated wires with a fine alloy bridge wire connected and a gun-cotton wisp in contact with the fulminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After inserting plug and wires, dip fuse in waterproof composition and dry. Connect wires to a battery or electrical machine; current passes through the bridge wire, heats it, ignites the gun-cotton wisp, which ignites the fulminate. Keep ultimate explosives dry even if primers are kept wet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired requisites for an ideal military high explosive
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal high explosive should combine great power in small compass, permanency under tropical heat, ease of firing when slightly confined, safety from neighboring explosions and projectile impact, and resistance to water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate new explosive agents (e.g., gelatine) against these requisites: permanence at heat, reliable detonation under confinement, safety when adjacent charges explode, tolerance to water exposure, and not detonating from projectile impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility of explosive combinations (gelatine and gun-cotton)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine collodion gun-cotton with nitro-glycerine (≈7% gun-cotton to 93% nitro-glycerine) to form explosive gelatine which is elastic, water-resistant, and less liable to separate nitro-glycerine under pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the collodion variety of gun-cotton (not ordinary explosive gun-cotton) finely shredded and dissolved in nitro-glycerine at ~80° F with constant stirring. Gelatine resists water, tolerates projectile impact, and requires confinement for full detonation; addition of up to ~4–6% camphor can raise decomposition temperature without materially reducing strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding contamination and impurities to prevent spontaneous decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Impurities, especially residual acids or impure reactants, are principal causes of decomposition and accidental explosions; ensure complete washing and use of pure materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All accidents mentioned are ascribed to imperfect washing or impure reactants. Maintain stringent washing protocols and use pure feedstocks; constantly monitor process parameters (temperature, agitation, washing completeness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate uses of different explosive types
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose explosive type according to intended application: gunpowder for firing guns, dynamite/gun-cotton/gelatine for mining, engineering, torpedoes, or bursting-charges—taking into account the violence and confinement behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High explosives (nitro-glycerine, dynamite, gun-cotton, gelatine) are excellent for mining and engineering (e.g., Hoosac Tunnel) but generally unsuited to propel projectiles from guns because their sudden action can burst the piece; use unconfined or tamping strategies as appropriate and avoid using bursting charges in guns unless specially designed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation and fume control during nitration
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure effective ventilation to remove nitrous fumes and protect workers during acid reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overhead hood and chimney draft with furnace fire to draw off fumes; keep acid pitchers in ice-cooled troughs and force a stream of cold dry air through pitchers to maintain agitation and dissipate heat and fumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing and monitoring during manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously monitor reaction temperature and material states during manufacture to prevent overheating or under-processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try each pitcher with a thermometer at short intervals during nitration; experienced workman judges charcoal roasting endpoint by sight; monitor drying, pressing pressures (e.g., ~15,000 psi final pressure for gun-cotton pressing), and washing completeness.
